questions.stem: Why does a transformer need positional encoding at all?
choices: To reduce the number of parameters
Because self-attention is permutation-invariant: without positional information the model would treat a sentence as an unordered set of tokens
To normalise the embeddings
To mask padding tokens
questions.explanation: Attention computes a weighted sum over all positions with no inherent notion of order, so shuffling the input would leave the representation unchanged. Positional encoding injects order into the embeddings before the first attention layer. Recurrent and convolutional models get order for free from their structure; transformers must add it.

questions.stem: In scaled dot-product attention, what roles do the query, key and value play?
choices: Query and key produce the relevance weights; those weights are applied to the values to form the output
Query produces the output directly and key and value are discarded
All three are identical by definition
Key holds the output and query holds the gradient
questions.explanation: The query is compared against every key by dot product to score relevance; those scores are softmaxed into weights and used to average the values. Splitting 'what am I looking for' (query), 'what do I offer for matching' (key) and 'what do I contribute' (value) is the core of the mechanism.

questions.stem: Why are the dot products divided by the square root of the key dimension?
choices: To keep the result under one
Because dot-product magnitude grows with dimension, pushing softmax into saturated regions where gradients vanish
To make the computation faster
To normalise the output to unit length
questions.explanation: For large key dimensions the dot products have large variance, so softmax produces near one-hot distributions with vanishingly small gradients. Dividing by the square root of the dimension keeps the variance roughly constant, which is exactly why the mechanism is called *scaled* dot-product attention.

questions.stem: What does self-attention mean, as distinct from attention in general?
choices: The model attends to its own parameters
Queries, keys and values all come from the same sequence, so each position attends to the other positions of that same input
Attention is computed without a softmax
Only the first token is attended to
questions.explanation: In self-attention a sequence relates to itself, letting each token gather context from every other token in the same input. Cross-attention, by contrast, draws queries from one sequence and keys and values from another — which is how a decoder consults the encoder in a translation model.

questions.stem: What does multi-head attention add over a single attention head?
choices: It runs attention several times in parallel in different learned subspaces, letting the model capture several kinds of relationship at once
It makes the model deeper
It removes the need for positional encoding
It reduces the parameter count to one head's worth
questions.explanation: Each head projects into its own subspace and learns its own notion of relevance — one may track syntactic dependency, another coreference. Their outputs are concatenated and projected back. A single head must compress all relationship types into one attention pattern.

questions.stem: Which task suits a transformer encoder stack rather than a decoder stack?
choices: Free-form text generation
Sentence classification, where the whole input is available and a bidirectional representation helps
Autoregressive completion
Streaming token-by-token output
questions.explanation: An encoder sees the entire sequence in both directions, which is ideal for building a representation to classify or extract from. Generation requires that a position not see the future, which is what the decoder's causal mask enforces.

questions.stem: What does the causal (look-ahead) mask do in a decoder, and why is it necessary during training?
choices: It hides padding tokens from attention
It prevents each position from attending to later positions, so the model cannot see the answer it is being asked to predict
It masks a random 15% of tokens
It limits the context window
questions.explanation: Because the whole target sequence is fed in at once for efficiency, without a causal mask position i could simply read position i+1 and the next-token objective would be trivial. The mask enforces the left-to-right condition that also holds at inference. Padding masks and the 15% masking of BERT are different mechanisms.

questions.stem: What is BERT's masked language modelling objective?
choices: Predicting the next sentence
Randomly masking a proportion of input tokens and training the model to recover them from bidirectional context
Predicting the next token left to right
Masking the output layer during fine-tuning
questions.explanation: MLM corrupts the input by masking roughly 15% of tokens and asks the model to restore them using context from both sides. That bidirectional objective is what makes BERT's representations strong for understanding tasks, and also what makes it unsuitable for free generation.

questions.stem: What is next sentence prediction (NSP) in BERT's pretraining?
choices: Generating the following sentence
A binary classification of whether sentence B actually follows sentence A in the source corpus
Predicting the masked tokens of the next sentence
Ranking candidate next sentences
questions.explanation: NSP pairs sentences, half genuinely consecutive and half randomly sampled, and trains a binary classifier on the pooled representation. The aim was to teach inter-sentence relationships for tasks like question answering, though later work found its contribution smaller than MLM's.

questions.stem: Which TWO special tokens does BERT use and what for?
choices: [CLS] at the start, whose final representation is used for sequence-level classification
[SEP] to separate segments and mark the end of a sequence
[MASK] to mark the end of the vocabulary
[PAD] to indicate the beginning of a sentence
questions.explanation: [CLS] gives a fixed position whose output can serve as a whole-sequence summary, and [SEP] delimits segments for sentence-pair tasks. [MASK] exists but marks tokens to be predicted, not vocabulary boundaries, and [PAD] fills to a common batch length rather than marking sentence starts.

questions.stem: What does a residual (skip) connection around a sublayer accomplish?
choices: It reduces the model's parameter count
It adds the sublayer's input to its output, giving gradients a direct path and making deep stacks trainable
It masks padding
It normalises the attention weights
questions.explanation: Residual connections let the gradient flow around each sublayer rather than only through it, which is what makes stacking dozens of layers feasible. Combined with layer normalisation they are the reason transformer depth trains stably.

questions.stem: What is the position-wise feed-forward network inside a transformer block?
choices: A recurrent layer applied across positions
A small MLP applied independently and identically to each position after attention
An attention layer with a single head
A pooling operation over the sequence
questions.explanation: After attention mixes information across positions, the feed-forward network transforms each position on its own with shared weights. The division of labour is deliberate: attention moves information between positions, the MLP processes it within a position.

questions.stem: Why does self-attention cost grow quadratically with sequence length?
choices: Because the feed-forward layers scale quadratically
Because every position computes a score against every other position, producing an N by N attention matrix
Because positional encodings are quadratic
Because the vocabulary grows with length
questions.explanation: The attention matrix has one entry per pair of positions, so both compute and memory scale with the square of the length. This is the central obstacle to long contexts and the reason for sparse, linear and state-space alternatives.

questions.stem: In an encoder-decoder transformer used for translation, what does cross-attention do?
choices: Lets decoder positions attend to the encoder's output representations of the source sentence
Lets encoder positions attend to each other
Attends across batch elements
Attends across attention heads
questions.explanation: Cross-attention is how the decoder consults the source: queries come from the decoder state while keys and values come from the encoder output. Encoder self-attention relates source positions to each other, and decoder self-attention relates generated positions to each other.

questions.stem: In PyTorch, why is nn.TransformerEncoderLayer typically stacked with nn.TransformerEncoder rather than used alone?
choices: A single layer cannot compute attention
Depth is what gives the model capacity to build progressively more abstract representations; one layer captures only shallow relationships
It is required for the optimiser to work
A single layer cannot be moved to a GPU
questions.explanation: Each layer refines the representation produced by the one below, so stacking builds hierarchy: lower layers tend to capture surface and syntactic structure, higher layers more semantic relationships. TransformerEncoder is simply the container that repeats the layer N times.

questions.stem: A decoder-only model trained for causal language modelling is asked to classify sentiment. What is the standard adaptation?
choices: It cannot be used for classification at all
Frame the task as generation — prompt it to emit a label — or attach a classification head to the final token's representation
Remove the causal mask and retrain from scratch
Convert it to an encoder by reversing the layers
questions.explanation: Decoder-only models handle classification either by generating the label as text, which is how prompting works, or by adding a head on the last position's hidden state and fine-tuning. Neither requires abandoning the architecture; removing the causal mask would invalidate everything the model learned.

questions.stem: What is layer normalisation doing in a transformer block?
choices: Normalising across the batch dimension
Normalising each position's feature vector to zero mean and unit variance, stabilising training independently of batch size
Normalising the attention weights to sum to one
Normalising the learning rate
questions.explanation: Layer norm operates within a single example across its features, which is why it suits variable-length sequences and small batches where batch normalisation behaves poorly. Softmax already normalises attention weights; that is a separate operation.

questions.stem: Which TWO changes would you expect to help a transformer that underfits a translation task?
choices: Increase model depth or width to add capacity
Train for longer with a suitable learning-rate schedule and warmup
Add stronger dropout
Reduce the training set size
questions.explanation: Underfitting means the model has not captured the structure present in the data, so the remedies add capacity or give optimisation more opportunity to converge; transformers in particular are sensitive to warmup. Stronger dropout and less data both reduce effective capacity, which is the opposite of what underfitting needs.

questions.stem: Why does BERT mask roughly 15% of tokens rather than a much higher proportion?
choices: Because the tokenizer cannot handle more
Because too much masking leaves too little context to reconstruct from, while too little makes the task trivial and training inefficient
Because 15% is the vocabulary ratio
Because higher rates break the attention mask
questions.explanation: The masking rate trades signal against context. Mask too much and the remaining text cannot support reconstruction; mask too little and most positions contribute no learning signal per pass. The 15% figure is an empirical balance, not a structural constraint.
